toc.title: What a polyvagal-informed therapist can offer

sections.title: A focus on your capacity to feel safe and present
Co-regulation, starting with the therapist's own state
Seeing you as stuck, not broken
Warmth instead of a blank slate

toc.title: How to find a polyvagal-informed therapist

blocks.p: You've set out on a path toward healing and self-discovery. You've probably crossed paths with a lot of ways of doing that: therapy, coaching, courses, and more. And within those are more paths still, like cognitive behavioral therapy, dialectical behavioral therapy, somatic experiencing, internal family systems, psychoanalysis, and so on. There's a new pathway to recovering from trauma everywhere you turn.

If you've gone deep enough, you've probably come across Polyvagal Theory and wondered how a polyvagal therapist could help you. To answer that, you first need to understand what Polyvagal Theory is, and get clear on what a polyvagal therapist is, if anything.

The basic idea, for our purposes here, is that Polyvagal Theory proposes three branches of the autonomic nervous system. These branches can be basically on or off. Yes, it's way more complex, but for our purposes we can see them as on or off. When they're activated, they result in different experiences: emotional, cognitive, sensations, all kinds of things.

ul: The ventral vagal parasympathetic branch is responsible for social behaviors and emotions when you're safe.
The sympathetic branch is responsible for flight and fight behaviors when you're in danger.
The dorsal vagal parasympathetic branch is responsible for shutdown and immobility when you're under life threat.

blocks.p: Polyvagal Theory is much more complex than that, but it's a good enough overview for now. At a minimum, I'd say a polyvagal therapist understands the state of their client's body, and how prepared it is for safety or for defense.
This is me nitpicking, but I think "polyvagal informed" is a better title than "polyvagal therapist." Polyvagal therapist sounds appropriate, but it's a little misleading.

No therapist that I know of is directly measuring the state of their client's autonomic nervous system. There are no monitors and no gadgets, as far as I know. There is one exception: it was released very quietly, and I've never seen or heard of anyone actually using it, but there's an orb that lights up during a therapy session based on what it detects from the client's polyvagal state. I have my questions and my thoughts about it, and I can't attest to how accurate it is. So technically there is a measurement device out there. But for the most part, the rest of us have to make inferences about our client's polyvagal state.

That's why polyvagal informed fits better. It means we understand Polyvagal Theory, which is a biological theory. But we're not polyvagal scientists measuring polyvagal state or heart rate variability.
Polyvagal Theory is science. It's not a prescription and it's not a modality. So there's really no one right way to be a polyvagal-informed therapist.

Polyvagal Theory helps us understand our client's state and their capacity for change. But there are no prescriptions, no set of techniques like with cognitive behavioral therapy, no manual. A therapist can be polyvagal informed and use that knowledge within their own therapeutic modality. A somatic therapist can use their Polyvagal Theory knowledge, and so can a psychoanalytic therapist. I do think Polyvagal Theory probably fits better with some modalities than others, especially ones more grounded in mindfulness and mind-body, somatic interventions.

blocks.h: What a polyvagal-informed therapist can offer

blocks.p: Not every polyvagal-informed therapist will use their knowledge the same way, so it's tough to say exactly what you'll get. But here are some benefits I'd expect.

blocks.h3: A focus on your capacity to feel safe and present

blocks.p: A polyvagal-informed therapist should have a really keen understanding of the safety state and how important it is, and bring that knowledge into the session. So there's going to be more focus on your present moment experience, and on your ability to be present and in your safety state.

blocks.h3: Co-regulation, starting with the therapist's own state

blocks.p: A polyvagal-informed therapist is going to provide co-regulation to help you feel safe and present. Any therapist who does the basic therapy skills probably does that. But I'd hope a polyvagal-informed therapist prioritizes their own self-regulation, their own safety state, to make sure they're actually providing co-regulation.

In some therapies the therapist is supposed to be the expert, more of a blank slate. In those, the therapist probably isn't going to prioritize their own self-regulation. They'll prioritize analysis, or insight building, or being the expert who tells the client what's happening within them, rather than working with the client collaboratively. Part of working collaboratively is the therapist being self-regulated, grounded in their safety state, and giving co-regulating safety cues. In my opinion, that should cross every therapeutic modality.

This therapist understands that the relationship is the most important facet of therapy, and studies have shown this numerous times. They understand they're not simply the expert in psychology. The relationship, the co-regulation, is instrumental to the client's success. It's not all of it, but it's a good chunk of it, and it gives the client a healthy platform to use as a springboard for change.

Deb Dana put it this way on the podcast: "We need enough experiences of safe co-regulation first and for many clients they've missed that. People have been dangerous and the therapist is taking on that role of being the first safe co-regulator in their life." ([Episode 54](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/98a53db3-770b-483d-ad74-40256d4c6b3a))

A polyvagal-informed therapist should be able to meet you where you are in your capacity to keep going with difficult material. Any therapist could do this, but a polyvagal therapist should recognize when you're losing access to your safety state, losing access to your present moment experience, losing that grounding in the present.

They're probably more likely to recognize body language and shifts in energy. You might get more fidgety or more anxious, lose eye contact, or your voice might go more monotone. A polyvagal therapist should pick up on those things, recognize them cognitively, understand what's happening, and adjust their interventions. A therapist who isn't polyvagal informed could still do that without the cognitive knowledge. They might just be a very empathetic, compassionate person who knows these things intuitively.
Dr. Porges described what that awareness asks of a therapist when he was on the podcast:

q: They really need to be truly Polyvagal informed. And what does that mean? It means they have to be aware of the state that their client is in.
blocks.cite: Stephen Porges, [From Sound to Safety: Understanding the Safe & Sound Protocol (episode 254)](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/20b541da-11ef-4b2e-b911-42b6ceba2bd1)

blocks.h3: Seeing you as stuck, not broken

blocks.p: A polyvagal-informed therapist is hopefully going to deeply understand your present-moment experiences in light of your current and past circumstances. They'll see you as someone in a dysregulated or stuck defensive state. Other therapists might see a chemical imbalance, or something genetic and passed down, or they might see you through the lens of whatever modality they use. Those things could still connect. But I think a polyvagal-informed therapist is going to see you as someone who shifts into and out of defensive states, someone capable of accessing their safety state and being in the present moment, and someone whose mental health "symptoms" can ease as they do.

Any therapist should be able to offer compassion without judgment. To me, that's a basic skill. But I'd hope a polyvagal-informed therapist goes further, seeing you as someone stuck in a defensive state, or someone who has gone through an autonomic state shift they can't quite shift out of yet. That therapist sees someone who isn't making a conscious choice and can't will themselves out of their stuck state. Other therapists might see the problem as not thinking correctly, or simply needing to change behavior.

A therapist using a cognitive or behavioral style can still do good work. But if they're polyvagal informed, they'll see a deeper layer underneath the behavior and the cognitions that needs to be addressed. Once that's addressed, the cognitions and behaviors can probably be addressed more effectively.

blocks.h3: Warmth instead of a blank slate

blocks.p: A polyvagal-informed therapist is probably less likely to use a neutral, unemotional presence. I think people expect their therapist to be a neutral, flat, blank slate. That's how we've traditionally viewed therapists, and if you're a student in therapy school, you might be taught that showing emotion isn't good.

Instead, I think a polyvagal-informed therapist is more likely to be genuine, their real self, from a well-regulated place. They'll use their face and their voice to convey warmth and safety, and to be compassionate. They won't shy away from expressing emotion. They're also not going to take over the session crying and sharing their own stuff. That's basic therapy: not too much self-disclosure, not dominating the session with your own emotions. A polyvagal-informed therapist can express what they're feeling, in words and in their face and voice, while keeping access to their safety state and their compassion.

I think a polyvagal-informed therapist is more likely to go beyond the thoughts and emotions you express, and to work with the internal sensations and impulses in your body. A lot of therapists focus on thinking and behavior, and that can be frustrating for both therapist and client, because there's more going on.

A polyvagal-informed therapist will work with thoughts, behavior, and emotion, and also with sensations and impulses. It's more holistic. They'll bring in spirituality and support systems, all the basic therapy pieces. But they'll look deeper into your present moment experience, including the internal sensations and impulses that come from your polyvagal state.

blocks.h: How to find a polyvagal-informed therapist

blocks.p: It's possible, but you'll have to do some research. It isn't widespread. For you and me this is a big part of our lives, but for most therapists and most people, Polyvagal Theory isn't a topic of conversation. No one's really getting trained in it. Therapists kind of have to seek it out. I've heard there are some graduate-level courses teaching Polyvagal Theory here and there, and it's growing, but I don't think it's a common or standard part of graduate curriculum. Typically, it means a therapist is doing their own continuing education.
Here's how to look:

ol: Search for licensed therapists in your area, through Psychology Today or a Google search.
Vet them. Check out their website and their social media. See what they say about Polyvagal Theory in particular. See if they have a blog or a podcast where they share what they know.

Use their content as a screening. This takes more time, and it's more of a challenge. The good news is that if you find someone, you can spend a lot of time with them through their content well ahead of time. You see how they think about things and how they talk, and you get a sense of how much warmth they have or don't have. If this matters to you, I think it's worth it.

Check licensing. In the United States, you'll need a licensed therapist in your state, since therapists aren't necessarily licensed to work outside their state. If the right person in your state is too far away, virtual sessions are a really good option.

blocks.p: If you can't find a polyvagal-informed therapist, there are other options.

ul: Share it with your current therapist. I've heard from podcast listeners and community members who have shared this information with their therapist. If you feel comfortable doing so, the free Polyvagal Theory episodes 101 through 109 are a good starting point to point them to.

Work with a polyvagal-informed coach. I worked with a coach who was polyvagal informed, and she was great. One caveat: do your vetting and screening, because anyone can call themselves a coach. Coaching isn't therapy, but depending on your level of need, it might be a good option.

Work with a somatic experiencing practitioner. These practitioners aren't necessarily therapists or coaches. Somatic experiencing is its own modality, though a practitioner could also be a therapist or coach. I think it's pretty common for them to have a good knowledge of Polyvagal Theory. Somatic experiencing is a trauma treatment modality, and from what I've seen from the outside, and from looking at some of their materials, it seems great. Peter Levine created somatic experiencing, and he is fantastic.

Take a course. Depending on your level of need, maybe you don't need therapy. Maybe you need a course or two. If you do well learning new concepts and being guided through a course structure, look for polyvagal-informed courses. The main source I'd point to for Polyvagal Theory education is the Polyvagal Institute. They offer a lot of courses. Many are for providers, but a few are for people who just want to learn about Polyvagal Theory, and prices range from about 50 to 300 bucks to own a course. One possible limitation: they teach Polyvagal Theory, and I'm sure they do a fantastic job, but they aren't geared toward trauma recovery exactly. I don't think you can go there expecting a trauma recovery course.
